children: Global portfolio reallocations add to the pressure, while the Rs 30,213 crore IPO of Jio Platforms temporarily absorbs liquidity from the market

Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have withdrawn Rs 48,056 crore from Indian equities in October so far, taking their cumulative outflows for 2026 to Rs 3.08 lakh crore, as elevated crude oil prices, geopolitical tensions and concerns over corporate earnings continue to weigh on investor sentiment.

The latest withdrawals have already surpassed the Rs 1.66 lakh crore pulled out by overseas investors during the whole of 2025, highlighting the sustained pressure on Indian markets from global capital flows. However, the pace of selling showed signs of easing last week, with FPIs turning net buyers in two trading sessions.

The October outflows follow net withdrawals of Rs 35,861 crore in September. Foreign investors had previously invested Rs 20,200 crore in Indian equities in July and Rs 29,631 crore in August, according to data from Central Depository Services (CDSL).

“For the week ended 23 October FIIs significantly reduced their selling and even turned buyers on two days. The moderation in US bond yields with the 10-year yield declining from 5.36 per cent to around 5 per cent, appreciation in the rupee to 94.94 to the dollar and the low valuations, particularly of the large-caps, contributed to the moderation in FII selling,” said V K Vijayakumar, Chief Investment Strategist, Geojit Investments.

Several factors have contributed to the persistent selling, including uncertainty surrounding conflicts in the Middle East, inflation concerns and relatively weak corporate earnings. Global portfolio reallocations have added to the pressure, while the Rs 30,213-crore initial public offering (IPO) of Jio Platforms temporarily absorbed liquidity from the market.
Although corporate earnings for the second quarter have been relatively strong, rising crude oil and logistics costs could erode margins and constrain earnings growth in the coming quarters.

The moderation in FPI selling towards the end of the month offers some relief to domestic equities, but sustained foreign investor participation will depend partly on how global economic and geopolitical risks evolve.
FIIs Remain Selective In Debt Markets

Overseas investors also remained net sellers in the Indian debt market during October so far, although flows varied across investment routes. FPIs withdrew Rs 3,858 crore through the Fully Accessible Route (FAR) and Rs 1,332 crore through the Voluntary Retention Route (VRR). In contrast, they invested Rs 3,737 crore through the general investment route.

“FAR saw net selling of about Rs 2,240 crore, and most of it came in one go, Rs 2,442 crore on Friday’s report alone, one of the biggest single-day FAR outflows this month. VRR was a steady seller too, while the general limit was mixed. Friday’s report as a whole showed about Rs 3,020 crore of debt outflows,” said Dheeraj Gaur, Chief Investment Strategy Officer, Choice Wealth.

The 10-year G-sec ended the week at about 7.47 per cent, a 3-year high, and the spread over the US 10-year is around 251 bps, the widest in four months. On paper that should tempt foreign buyers. In practice, apparently, they want a steadier rupee more than they want extra carry, and the RBI’s liquidity tightening, inflation concerns, on top of its 07 October rate hike, is keeping yields high without yet winning them over, Gaur added.
The divergence in debt flows suggests that foreign investors have continued to adjust their exposure to Indian assets amid uncertainty over the global economic outlook.
Crude Oil, US GDP, Geopolitics In Focus

Market direction in the coming sessions is likely to depend on a combination of macroeconomic data, geopolitical developments and corporate earnings. US gross domestic product (GDP) data will be a key indicator for investors assessing the health of the world’s largest economy and its implications for global financial markets.

“Going ahead, the steady moderation in FII selling offers some comfort, though elevated crude and sharp broader-market weakness keep the downside risk alive. Market participants will closely monitor the US Federal Reserve’s FOMC policy decision and the Bank of Japan’s rate decision in the coming week,” said Pabitro Mukherjee, Deputy Vice President-Research, Bajaj Broking.

On the macroeconomic front, US GDP data will be a key focus, while movements in Brent crude prices, developments in the US-Iran and Russia-Ukraine conflicts, and ongoing quarterly earnings will remain key drivers of investor sentiment, Mukherjee added.
